title: “GOD TOLD ME…” — BUT WHAT IF GOD NEVER SAID IT?
paragraphs: “GOD TOLD ME…” — BUT WHAT IF GOD NEVER SAID IT?
The most dangerous deception may not be the voice that tells you to abandon God, but the one that sounds spiritual enough to make you believe you are obeying Him.
Imagine spending years defending a decision God never asked you to make.
Imagine breaking someone's heart, walking away from a responsibility, entering the wrong relationship, or destroying a friendship because you were absolutely convinced that God had spoken.
And then, somewhere between the consequences and the tears, a terrifying question enters your mind.
Was that really God… or was that me?

Perhaps you wanted something so desperately that every coincidence became confirmation. Every emotional experience became revelation. Every open door became divine permission. Every person who questioned you became an obstacle the enemy had sent.
You prayed, but perhaps you were not genuinely asking God what He wanted.
You were asking Him to approve what you had already decided.
And that is where spiritual deception becomes dangerously personal.
Few statements carry as much weight among Christians as the words, “God told me.”

Those three words can comfort the broken, encourage the weary, and inspire courageous obedience when spoken truthfully. But when misused, they can manipulate people, silence accountability, justify sinful behavior, and attach the authority of heaven to the desires of a human heart.
Someone says, “God told me you are supposed to marry me.”
Another says, “God told me to leave my spouse.”
A preacher declares, “God told me that you must give this amount of money.”
Someone refuses correction because, supposedly, God has already confirmed everything.
But since when did claiming to hear God make someone incapable of being wrong?
The Bible never teaches us to abandon discernment simply because something sounds spiritual.
In fact, it commands the opposite.
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” — 1 John 4:1, KJV
The original Greek reads:
Μὴ παντὶ πνεύματι πιστεύετε, ἀλλὰ δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα εἰ ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν.
Mē panti pneumati pisteuete, alla dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou theou estin.
A close translation is, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to determine whether they are from God.”
The Greek word δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete) means to examine, test, or assess something to determine its genuineness.
John is not encouraging unbelief. In the immediate context, he is warning believers about false prophets and teachings that deny the truth concerning Jesus Christ.
Biblical faith is not gullibility.
Discernment is not rebellion.
Testing a spiritual claim is not an insult to God. It is obedience to His written Word.

Paul reinforces this in 1 Thessalonians 5:19–22. He tells believers not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecies, but also commands them to examine everything, hold firmly to what is good, and abstain from evil.
Notice the balance.
Do not reject everything.
Do not believe everything.
Test everything.
God's truth does not become less true when examined.
Perhaps one of the hardest realities to accept is that sincerity does not guarantee accuracy.
You can sincerely believe something and still be mistaken.
You can cry during worship, feel chills while praying, experience an extraordinary dream, and still misunderstand what those experiences mean.
Your emotions are real, but your interpretation of them may be wrong.
A powerful feeling is not automatically a prophetic revelation.
An inner voice is not automatically the Holy Spirit.
A coincidence is not automatically divine confirmation.
And peace is not always proof that you are making the right decision.
Sometimes obedience brings peace. Sometimes it brings trembling knees, sleepless nights, sacrifice, and tears.
Jesus Himself experienced profound anguish in Gethsemane.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
In Greek:
Πλὴν μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω.
Plēn mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō.
“Nevertheless, let not my will, but yours, be done.”
That is the posture of genuine surrender.
Jesus was not searching for emotional comfort as the final confirmation of the Father's will. He submitted to the Father even when obedience meant suffering.
Sometimes the clearest evidence of spiritual maturity is not how confidently you declare that God has spoken.
It is how willingly you surrender when His written Word contradicts what you desperately want.
Jeremiah 17:9 contains a sobering description of the human heart.
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿAqov hallev mikkol, ve'anush hu, mi yeda'ennu.
The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick; who can understand it?
The Hebrew word עָקֹב (ʿaqov) carries the sense of being deceitful or crooked.
The following verse reminds us that the Lord searches the heart and examines the inner person.
God understands motives we have not yet recognized in ourselves.
That is why our desires must be surrendered to Him rather than automatically treated as messages from Him.
Loneliness can influence what you believe God is saying about a relationship.
Anger can disguise itself as righteous indignation.
Ambition can masquerade as divine calling.
Fear can sound like spiritual caution.
Pride can convince you that you are too anointed to be corrected.
And bitterness can make revenge feel like divine justice.
Not every mistaken impression is demonic. Sometimes it is simply human weakness, misunderstanding, emotional exhaustion, or an unexamined desire.
That is precisely why we need grace, humility, Scripture, and accountability.
Think about the religious leaders in Jesus' day.
They possessed extensive knowledge of Scripture. They spoke about God. They maintained religious traditions. Yet many opposed the very Messiah to whom the Scriptures testified.
Jesus told them:
“Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” — John 5:39–40, KJV
It is possible to speak constantly about God while resisting the truth He has revealed.
It is possible to use Scripture without submitting to its message.
Even Satan quoted Scripture when tempting Jesus in the wilderness.
In Matthew 4, the devil cited Psalm 91 while attempting to persuade Jesus to throw Himself from the temple.
Jesus answered with Scripture rightly applied.
“It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” — Matthew 4:7, KJV
The presence of a Bible verse did not make the temptation holy.
Context mattered.
Truth mattered.
The character and will of God mattered.
So when someone tells you that God has spoken, or when you believe you have received personal direction, begin with what God has already revealed in Scripture.
God will not contradict His own truth to accommodate your desires.
He will not authorize adultery because a relationship feels destined.
He will not command dishonesty because financial success appears to be waiting on the other side.
He will not give someone permission to manipulate another person's conscience in His name.
He will not redefine sin simply because obedience has become inconvenient.
Second Timothy 3:16 describes Scripture using the Greek word θεόπνευστος (theopneustos), meaning God-breathed.
Scripture possesses divine authority and equips believers for faithful living.
Our personal impressions must remain subject to that authority.
Not the other way around.
But what about decisions that Scripture does not address individually?
Which job should you accept? Whom should you marry? Should you move somewhere new? Should you begin a ministry?
Scripture may not provide a specific name, address, or employment contract, but it provides the moral boundaries, wisdom, priorities, and principles through which those decisions should be examined.
James 1:5 encourages believers to ask God for wisdom.
Proverbs 15:22 teaches the value of receiving counsel.
Romans 12:2 connects discernment with the transformation and renewal of the mind.
You do not need to manufacture a supernatural announcement for every decision.
Sometimes faithful decision-making involves prayer, biblical wisdom, careful consideration, trustworthy counsel, and the freedom to choose responsibly before God.
And sometimes the most spiritually responsible thing you can say is:
“I believe God may be leading me in this direction, but I am still praying, examining Scripture, and seeking wisdom.”
There is humility in those words.
There is room for correction.
There is an acknowledgment that God is infallible, but your understanding is not.
Examine also the fruit of what you believe you have heard.
James 3:17 describes wisdom from above as pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, and sincere.
The Greek word εὐπειθής (eupeithēs) conveys the idea of being willing to listen or open to persuasion.
Consider that carefully.
Heavenly wisdom is not characterized by an arrogant refusal to listen.
When every question makes you angry, every correction feels like persecution, and every disagreement becomes evidence that others lack spiritual discernment, something deserves examination.
That does not mean everyone who questions you is right. Jesus Himself faced unjust opposition.
But genuine spiritual conviction does not require you to declare yourself beyond accountability.
In 1 Corinthians 14:29, Paul instructs that prophets may speak and that others should weigh what is said.
Even within a congregation exercising prophetic gifts, discernment was expected.
Christians differ in their understanding of how prophetic gifts operate today. Some believe such gifts continue; others understand their role differently in light of the completion of Scripture.
But neither position gives anyone permission to elevate personal impressions above biblical authority.
And nobody has the right to control your life simply by announcing, “God told me.”
If someone uses those words to pressure you into marriage, sexual activity, financial giving, secrecy, isolation, or unquestioning submission, you are allowed to ask questions.
You are allowed to seek independent counsel.
You are allowed to establish boundaries.
You are allowed to refuse manipulation.
God's name must never become a weapon used to imprison another person's conscience.
Perhaps someone reading this has already been wounded by that kind of spiritual manipulation.
You trusted someone because they sounded anointed.
You surrendered your judgment because you were afraid that disagreeing with them meant disagreeing with God.
You gave what you could not afford.
You stayed where you were being harmed.
You carried guilt that Jesus never placed upon you.
And now you struggle to pray because the voice of the person who manipulated you has become tangled with your understanding of God.
Please hear this.
Someone misusing the name of Jesus does not mean Jesus has betrayed you.
The Shepherd is not identical to the person who falsely claimed to speak on His behalf.
Jesus warned about false prophets in Matthew 7:15–20. He taught that they would be recognized by their fruits.
In John 10:27, He said:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
The Greek reads:
Τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἐμὰ τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν, κἀγὼ γινώσκω αὐτά, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσίν μοι.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
In context, Jesus is describing the relationship between Himself and His sheep—their recognition of Him, their following Him, and the security He gives them.
This passage is not a guarantee that every thought entering a Christian's mind is a personal message from God.
The emphasis is on knowing and following Jesus.
Not becoming obsessed with decoding every feeling, dream, number, coincidence, or internal impression.
You do not have to live terrified that missing some mysterious sign will destroy God's entire purpose for your life.
Your Savior is not playing a cruel guessing game with your soul.
He has revealed His character.
He has given His Word.
He calls you to trust Him, repent of sin, walk in love, seek wisdom, and follow Him faithfully.
And when you discover that you have mistaken your own desires for His direction, the Gospel gives you somewhere to go.
Not into hiding.
Not into denial.
Not into another desperate attempt to justify yourself.
To the cross.
Perhaps you owe someone an apology.
Perhaps you need to admit that the decision you called divine revelation was actually your own.
Perhaps you need to stop defending something that has been hurting your family.
Perhaps the bravest words you could speak today are:
“I was wrong. I should never have claimed that God said something when I was not certain.”
There is no spiritual defeat in genuine repentance.
First John 1:9 reminds us that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
The Gospel does not require you to maintain the appearance of spiritual perfection.
It invites you to come honestly before a perfect Savior.
Peter once spoke with extraordinary confidence about his own faithfulness. He believed he was ready to follow Jesus even unto death.
Hours later, he denied Him.
Yet the risen Christ restored Peter in John 21.
His failure was not the end of his story.
And yours does not have to be either.
It means that the person who misused God's name can repent.
The person who was spiritually manipulated can find healing.
The believer who confused desire with revelation can grow in discernment.
The preacher who once resisted correction can learn humility.
The wounded Christian can rediscover the goodness of the Shepherd.
Grace does not make our mistakes harmless. It makes repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and transformation possible through Jesus Christ.
Have I ever said “God told me” because I was afraid to admit, “This is what I want”?
Have I ever used God's name to win an argument?
Have I ever rejected biblical correction because accepting it would cost me something?
Have I been following Jesus—or asking Jesus to follow my plans?
You do not need to publicly disclose the private details of your struggle.
Or simply write, “Give me discernment, Jesus.”

Somewhere among your friends may be someone quietly suffering under spiritual manipulation. Someone about to make a life-changing decision based entirely on an untested impression. Someone who desperately needs to know that asking honest questions does not make them a rebellious Christian.
We want to build a community where people are not merely emotionally moved by the Gospel but increasingly transformed by its truth.
Scripture teaches that giving should come from a willing heart.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
The Gospel is not for sale.
We support its proclamation because its message is worth spreading.
If you believe in what we are building and desire to help us continue reaching people with biblical truth, we would be grateful to have you partner with us.
And tonight, when you close your eyes and bring your unanswered questions before God, perhaps this should be your prayer:

Father, forgive me for the times I have confused my desires with Your direction. Forgive me for using Your name to defend my pride, my fears, or my decisions. Teach me to love Your truth more than I love being right. Give me wisdom to examine what I hear, humility to receive correction, courage to repent, and faith to obey Your Word even when obedience costs me something. Heal the wounds caused by those who have misused Your name. Renew my mind through Scripture. Let my life reflect the character of Jesus Christ. Not my will, Lord, but Yours be done. In Jesus' name, Amen.
You may never receive an extraordinary dream.
You may never experience a dramatic supernatural encounter.
You may never have a testimony that makes an entire room fall silent.
But you can know Jesus through the truth He has revealed.
You can walk faithfully with Him.
You can become someone whose words are trustworthy, whose heart is teachable, whose love is genuine, and whose life bears the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
And perhaps that is far more beautiful than constantly needing to announce that God has spoken.
Because spiritual maturity is not measured by how often you say, “God told me.”
It is revealed in how faithfully you obey what God has already made known.
Never become so desperate to hear something new from God that you stop listening to what He has already said.
